passage: I'm Sarika. When Irawati became our team lead in March, I was the first to hug her. By June something had shifted. She interrupted me twice in one stand-up, finished my sentences wrong, and began expecting the corner parking spot and first pick of leave dates. The others muttered about it in the pantry. I didn't join in, though I was tempted. I also knew her targets had doubled and her own boss called her at night. So one evening, walking to the bus stop, I said, "Ira, you've been cutting people off lately. I think the pressure's getting to you, but it's landing on us." She was quiet for a long stretch. Then: "I didn't realise. Will you tell me when I do it?" Looking back, I'm glad I said it to her and not about her.

qa.a: Irawati became our team lead in March.

qa.q: Why didn't Sarika join the muttering in the pantry?
qa.a: Sarika was tempted but felt sympathy for Irawati, knowing her targets had doubled and her boss called her at night.

qa.q: What choice did Sarika make on the walk to the bus stop, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sarika named the interrupting directly and kindly to Irawati while mentioning the pressure, so Irawati could hear it and asked to be told next time.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt hearing about the change?
qa.a: Irawati was probably surprised and a little stung, going quiet, but also open enough to ask Sarika to tell her when it happens 🙂

Note, 14 Aug. Devika, Class 3 teacher.
Manjula took over as primary coordinator in June. Things I've noticed since, written down so I don't turn them into staffroom gossip: she cut Rekha off mid-sentence twice at Monday's meeting; she no longer asks us before changing the exam timetable; yesterday she sent the peon to fetch her lunch first, ahead of everyone. The Manjula who shared my tiffin last year would have hated that. I also know the principal emails her at midnight and parents call her personal number.
What I did next: I asked her for tea after school, just the two of us. I said, "You've been interrupting people lately, and it's being noticed. I know you're being squeezed from above." She teared up a little, then laughed. She's asked me to nudge her ankle under the table at the next meeting.

qa.q: When did Manjula take over as primary coordinator?
qa.a: Manjula took over as primary coordinator in June.

qa.q: Why did Devika write the changes down?
qa.a: Devika wanted to keep track of what had changed without turning it into staffroom gossip, which shows a wish to be fair to Manjula.

qa.q: Which choice did Devika make instead of complaining, and how did it land?
qa.a: Devika asked Manjula for tea alone and named the interrupting while acknowledging the pressure; Manjula teared up, laughed, and asked for a nudge under the table.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha when Manjula cuts in mid-sentence?
qa.a: Rekha is likely to feel brushed aside and less willing to speak at meetings, which is part of why Devika's note matters.

12 Nov. Long day. Rajni's been floor manager for two months and today it really showed. In the huddle she talked over Gurpreet three times and then said, "Let's not waste time on feelings." She also took the window seat by the heater again, the one we used to take turns on. Old Rajni would have rolled her eyes at a manager like this. Ankit tried to get me to moan about her at the chai stall. I didn't. It's not fair either; she has the quality team breathing down her neck and a target that keeps going up. So at clock-out I waited and said, "Raj, you've stopped listening a bit. I get the pressure. I just miss you asking." She went quiet, then said, "Okay. Ouch. Fair." We shared an auto home. I think it landed.
— Jasleen

passage: At the milk cooperative in Wadgaon, Yusuf had always been the joker who helped everyone carry the cans. Then, at twenty-five, he was made collection-centre supervisor. Reena, who tested fat content at the next table, watched him change over two months. He began cutting farmers off mid-sentence when they queried a reading. He expected the first glass of tea from the stall boy, before the women who had been standing since five. In the meeting he talked over her twice. The other staff whispered about it by the chilling tank. Reena didn't join them. She also knew the dairy board now phoned him every evening about falling numbers. One afternoon, walking to the bus stand, she said, "Yusuf, you've stopped letting people finish. I think the board's pressure is getting to you, but the farmers feel it." passage: At the Pune logistics office, Joseph watched Tanvir take over as shift manager. They'd been friends since induction, cracking jokes over vada pav at the gate. Within two months, Tanvir started cutting people off mid-sentence, skipped the joint tea break, and expected the team to cover his late arrivals without a word. The team grumbled in the washroom. I don't think you mean to." Tanvir stiffened. "Head office is on my neck every day, Joseph." "I know. That's real. But the guys feel you've stopped hearing them." Tanvir exhaled, then said, "Tell me when I do it again." Joseph said he would.

Dear Gurleen,
I've been meaning to write for weeks, and I'd rather say this kindly than let it grow.
Since you became team lead, I've noticed small changes. You interrupt in meetings more. You don't join us for lunch. Last Friday, when Anil raised a concern, you said, "Just do it," and moved on. And you expect us to adjust around your schedule, which the old Gurleen would never have done.
I'm not writing because I'm angry. I know the pressure from the directors must be enormous; I've seen you working at midnight. It would change anyone.
But I miss the colleague who used to say, "Wait, let's hear everyone." I think the team does too. I'm telling you because you're my friend, not to complain.
Lunch on Monday?
Devika

qa.a: Gurleen said, "Just do it," and moved on.

qa.a: Devika feels caring but concerned, missing the old colleague and not wanting resentment to grow.

qa.a: It names specific changes kindly and privately, acknowledges the pressure, and invites reconnection, instead of gossiping.

qa.q: How might Gurleen react to the letter?
qa.a: Gurleen might feel stung at first, then perhaps grateful that a friend chose honesty over talking behind Gurleen's back.

I sat across from Joseph for two years before he was promoted. We were a team: ideas scribbled on the same notepad, shared biryani on Fridays.
After the promotion, he got a cabin. Slowly he changed. In meetings he finished other people's sentences. He started expecting reports on his desk before he asked. Once he snapped at a new joiner, "I don't have time for basic questions."
The others muttered about him at the tea machine. I didn't join in.
Instead, I waited till the end of a Friday and knocked. "Joseph, you've stopped letting people finish. The new joiner was upset."
He rubbed his eyes. "I know. The targets are killing me." He came out and apologised to the new joiner that evening.
I'm Devika. I still sit across from his cabin.

The others whispered in the laundry room. On the 24th, when he cut off a junior in front of a guest, Siami felt her face burn. She waited until the boiler mechanic had gone and caught Tenzin alone by the back stairs. 'You've stopped listening, Tenzin. To all of us. I miss my friend.' He opened his mouth to argue, then slumped against the wall. 'The owners call me every hour. I feel like if I'm soft, I'm finished.' Siami nodded. 'Then be tired with us. Not at us.'
